newsitem.title: USA: U.S. toxic waste cleanups taking longer - watchdog.
newsitem.headline: U.S. toxic waste cleanups taking longer - watchdog.

text.p: The pace of listing and cleaning up the worst U.S. toxic waste dumps has slowed over the last 10 years, the watchdog arm of Congress said Thursday.

The comments by the General Accounting Office (GAO) come at a time when House Republicans are questioning claims by the Clinton administration that its moves to reform the Superfund toxic waste program have speeded cleanups.
Republicans asked for the GAO review of Superfund progress to arm themselves for debates with the Environmental Protection Agency over proposals to overhaul the multibillion dollar program.

Peter Guerrero, a GAO director, told a House Government Reform and Oversight panel that the average time from discovery of a toxic waste site to a decision to add it to the Superfund list had risen from 5.8 years for sites listed in 1986 to 1990 to 9.4 years for sites added in 1996.
Part of the problem, according to the report, was that no sites had been listed between 1988 and 1992, which created a backlog to be reviewed.
EPA also cut in half funds for assessing sites between 1994 and 1996, shifting its focus to finishing cleanups at dumps that had already been listed, according to the GAO.
Actual cleanup times had grown steadily from an average of 3.9 years from 1986 to 1989 to an average of 10.6 years for sites cleaned in 1996, Guerrero said.

"EPA officials attributed the increased completion times for cleanups to the growing complexity of sites, efforts to reach settlements with parties responsible for site contamination, and resource constraints," he said, citing EPA responses to a report that GAO plans to submit next month.
GAO supported the view that cleanups were taking longer because they were becoming more difficult. Guerrero added that funding cuts had also affected EPA's work.
EPA Assistant Administrator Elliot Laws told the subcommittee that under EPA policy he could not comment publicly on a draft report by GAO or Guerrero's testimony.
But in his own testimony he highlighted that cleanups had been completed at 418 sites out of the more than 1,200 sites on the Superfund list, and EPA aimed to complete a total of 900 by 2000.
According to Democrats on the House subcommittee, 250 of those cleanups were finished over the last four years.
